\chapter*{Abstract}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Abstract}
\noindent
Air pollution in Indian cities regularly reaches hazardous concentrations,
and a forecast is useful only if it arrives before the hazardous day does.
This project forecasts daily PM2.5 one to three days ahead at a Delhi monitor
and evaluates the forecasts as a warning system rather than by average error
alone. The central finding is that the alarm budget a decision maker accepts
dominates the choice of model. Across ten specifications, from simple
benchmarks and a classical ARIMA model with annual Fourier terms to four
machine learning regressors and a recurrent network, the spread in hit rate
at a fixed alarm budget is about five percentage points, while moving the
budget from forty to one hundred alarms a year moves the hit rate by fifty.
Machine learning earns its place only partially. The classical model beats
every machine learning regressor at every horizon, a result strengthened
rather than weakened by a sensitivity analysis on the cleaning threshold, and
the one model that does win, a recurrent network, wins only at one day ahead,
reported as a range across seeds rather than a single favourable one. Two
real defects in the source monitor, a clipped instrument ceiling and a
miscalculated coverage statistic, were diagnosed and corrected before
modelling began. The recommendation is to design a warning system around its
alarm budget, treating the forecasting model as a secondary refinement.

\chapter{Introduction}
\label{chap:intro}

\section{Research Background}

Air pollution in Indian cities regularly reaches concentrations classified as
hazardous to human health. The public response to such episodes depends on
knowing that a severe day is coming before it arrives: a forecast issued on
the morning of a hazardous day is of limited value, while one issued a day or
more ahead can change behaviour, whether through health advisories,
restrictions on outdoor activity, or school closures. Daily pollution series
carry structure that makes such forecasting feasible in principle: persistence
from one day to the next, a strong annual cycle driven by meteorology and
seasonal agricultural burning, and dependence on recent local conditions.

My interest in this question is also personal. Having grown up in India, air
pollution was not an abstract statistic but part of ordinary life: seasonal
smog that turned daylight hazy, and days when going outside meant a sore
throat. Whether those days can be predicted reliably enough to be worth
warning people about is a question I have a genuine stake in.

\section{Research Problem}

Existing machine learning studies of Indian air quality (reviewed in
Chapter~\ref{chap:lit}) report forecast accuracy by average error, and do not
decompose that accuracy by the operating point at which a warning would
actually be raised. A model with respectable average error can still be a
poor warning system if it systematically misses the extreme days that are the
only ones anyone cares about, and the reverse also holds: two models with
very different average error can produce nearly identical warning
performance once a decision threshold is applied. Separately, the project
this report was proposed under assumed that daily pollution series carry a
weekly cycle alongside the annual one, driven by traffic and industrial
activity, and treated reconciling two seasonal periods as a central modelling
difficulty. Neither assumption is safe to carry into the modelling without
testing it directly, and both are tested in this report.

\section{Research Objectives}

\begin{enumerate}
\item To develop and evaluate a suite of classical, machine learning, and
deep learning models for forecasting daily PM2.5 concentrations one to three
days ahead at a single, well-characterised Indian monitoring station, under
an evaluation protocol that cannot leak future information into past
forecasts.
\item To compare two formulations of the hazardous-day warning problem:
forecasting the concentration and applying a health threshold to it, against
classifying the exceedance event directly.
\item To quantify forecast skill as a warning system, using hit rate and
false alarm rate under a varying decision threshold, rather than relying on
average error alone, and to establish how much of that skill is attributable
to the choice of model versus the choice of decision threshold.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Research Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item How accurately can daily concentrations be forecast one to three days
ahead by machine learning, relative to classical and naive benchmarks?
\item Is it better to forecast the concentration and then apply a threshold, or
to classify the exceedance event directly?
\item Considered as a warning system, what hit rate and false alarm rate does
each approach achieve, and how does the decision threshold trade them off?
\end{enumerate}

The answer to the third question turns out to dominate the other two, and the
report is organised accordingly.

\section{Research Significance}

The practical significance of this work is in the design of hazardous air
quality warning systems: the finding that the decision threshold dominates
the choice of model, developed in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} and
Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion}, implies that the alarm budget a health
authority is willing to raise is a more consequential design decision than
the forecasting model behind it. The methodological significance lies in
applying a leakage-tested rolling-origin evaluation, rather than a single
train-test split, to a model suite spanning classical statistics, machine
learning, and a deep recurrent architecture, on a dataset small enough that
the comparison between method families is itself informative about where
each is reliable.

\section{Structure of the Report}

Chapter~\ref{chap:lit} reviews the literature on air quality forecasting,
classical and machine learning methods for time series, deep learning methods
for time series, and forecast verification as a warning system.
Chapter~\ref{chap:method} describes the data, the two defects found in it,
and the full mathematical specification of every model fitted, organised
into machine learning methods and deep learning methods as the chapter's two
central sections, followed by the rolling-origin evaluation protocol.
Chapter~\ref{chap:results} presents the results against the three research
questions. Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion} interprets those results and states
the project's limitations. Chapter~\ref{chap:conclusion} concludes and
proposes future work.

\chapter{Literature Review}
\label{chap:lit}

\section{Air Quality Forecasting: Challenges and Characteristics}

Daily particulate matter series present a specific set of statistical
challenges that distinguish them from the time series most forecasting
methods were developed against. The distribution of PM2.5 concentrations is
strongly right skewed, with a small number of extreme episodes, rather than
normally distributed around a stable mean; the series is strongly seasonal
at the annual scale; and the quantity of practical interest, whether a day
exceeds a health threshold, is a minority class, typically under a third of
days even at a severe site. These three properties motivate working in
logarithms rather than on the raw concentration scale (Section~\ref{sec:arima}),
motivate testing rather than assuming the seasonal structure present in the
series (Section~\ref{sec:weekly}), and motivate evaluating forecasts as a
warning system rather than by a single average-error statistic
(Section~\ref{sec:verification}).

\section{Classical and Machine Learning Methods for Time Series Forecasting}
\label{sec:lit-ml}

The classical approach to a series with this structure is an autoregressive
integrated moving average (ARIMA) model, in which a series is differenced to
stationarity and then modelled as a linear combination of its own past values
and past forecast errors. Seasonal variants extend this by one additional
seasonal period, but a series with two seasonal periods, for instance a
weekly cycle and an annual one, cannot be accommodated by a single seasonal
ARIMA order, which is one of the two assumptions this project tests directly
rather than carrying over unexamined.

Machine learning offers an alternative that does not assume a linear
relationship between a forecast and its predictors. Penalised linear
regression controls the variance of an ordinary least squares fit by
shrinking its coefficients, which matters when predictors are highly
correlated, as lagged and rolling-window features of the same series
necessarily are \citep{hoerl1970ridge}. Random forests fit an ensemble of
decision trees to bootstrap-resampled data and average their predictions,
which reduces variance without the linearity assumption
\citep{breiman2001random}. Gradient boosting fits an ensemble additively,
each new tree correcting the residual error of the ensemble so far, which
historically gives better bias-variance trade-offs than a single tree or a
randomised ensemble on tabular data \citep{friedman2001gradient}. None of
these three methods assumes stationarity, a seasonal order, or a linear
functional form, which is their appeal relative to ARIMA; their cost is that
they fit the function empirically from a necessarily finite sample, and
\citet{makridakis2020m4} report, across 100{,}000 series in the M4
forecasting competition, that this flexibility does not reliably translate
into an advantage over classical benchmarks on series of a few thousand
observations, which is the order of magnitude available in this project.

\section{Deep Learning Methods for Time Series Forecasting}
\label{sec:lit-dl}

\subsection{Recurrent Neural Networks and the Vanishing Gradient Problem}

A recurrent neural network processes a sequence by maintaining a hidden
state that is updated at every timestep as a function of the current input
and the previous hidden state, which in principle lets it represent
dependence on the arbitrarily distant past without the fixed lag structure a
regression feature table imposes. In practice, a plain recurrent network
trained by backpropagation through time suffers from vanishing or exploding
gradients as the sequence lengthens, which makes it unable to learn
long-range dependence reliably \citep{hochreiter1997lstm}. The long
short-term memory (LSTM) architecture addressed this with a memory cell and
three multiplicative gates controlling what is written to, read from, and
forgotten by that cell, at the cost of a comparatively large number of
parameters for a short daily series.

\subsection{The Gated Recurrent Unit}

The gated recurrent unit (GRU) simplifies the LSTM to two gates and no
separate memory cell, while retaining the property that gradients can flow
across many timesteps without vanishing \citep{cho2014gru}. Its full
specification, and the specific architecture used in this project, is given
in Section~\ref{sec:gru}. The GRU's appeal for a daily series with roughly
three thousand observations is precisely its smaller parameter count relative
to an LSTM, which matters more on a dataset this size than the slightly
larger representational capacity an LSTM's extra gate and cell state provide.

\section{Machine Learning Applications to Delhi and Indian Air Quality}

Machine learning applied specifically to Delhi PM2.5 is not a new proposal.
\citet{masood2020delhi} fit several regression models directly to Delhi's
particulate record to predict concentrations, establishing that a standard
machine learning toolkit is applicable to this series at all.
\citet{singh2025stubble} narrow the same problem to the stubble burning
season, September to December, when biomass burning in neighbouring states
drives the city's most severe episodes, and frame their evaluation around
health risk rather than average error alone. Neither paper evaluates its
forecasts as a warning system in the sense used here, with an explicit alarm
budget and a false alarm rate reported alongside the hit rate; both report
accuracy on held-out data without decomposing it by the operating point at
which an alarm would actually be raised. That gap, between forecast accuracy
and warning system performance, is the space this project's third research
question occupies.

The finding that a classical benchmark beats every machine learning model in
this project's own results (Chapter~\ref{chap:results}) is not an anomaly
against the wider forecasting literature discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:lit-ml}. The mechanism \citet{makridakis2020m4} propose,
that a few thousand observations is a small sample for a flexible learner
relative to the number of parameters a modern architecture can fit, applies
directly to a project with roughly three thousand daily observations. The
negative result for machine learning at two and three days ahead in
Chapter~\ref{chap:results} is therefore the expected outcome under that
literature rather than a surprise specific to this dataset.

\section{Forecast Verification as a Warning System}
\label{sec:verification}

The distinction this project draws between forecast accuracy and warning
system performance, hit rate, false alarm rate, and the trade-off between
them as the decision threshold moves, follows the verification framework
standard in operational meteorology \citep{jolliffe2012forecast}. That
literature developed around exactly the situation faced here: a forecast of
a rare, high-impact event, where the average error of a model is a poor
guide to its value as a warning, and where a contingency table decomposed by
decision threshold is more informative than any single accuracy score. Its
central methodological point, that verification measures should be chosen to
match the decision a forecast supports rather than borrowed by default from
a different problem, motivated reporting hit rate and false alarm rate as a
pair in Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures} rather than a single skill score.

\section{Data Quality in Reference Air Quality Monitors}

The data quality problems documented in Section~\ref{sec:defects} are not
unique to this station. \citet{jiang2023negative} address the companion
problem to the one found here: reference monitors occasionally report
physically impossible negative PM2.5 concentrations, arising from instrument
noise near zero rather than a true measurement, and propose a defensible
statistical threshold below which a reading should be treated as invalid
rather than retained or naively clipped to zero. Their approach and the one
used in Section~\ref{sec:defects} for the clipped ceiling at 1990 share a
method rather than a target: both treat an implausible value as a data
quality question to be settled by evidence, specifically its relationship to
the plausible range and its recurrence pattern, rather than by a rule of
thumb applied uniformly. Considered together, artefacts at both ends of the
distribution suggest that reference-grade air quality monitors carry
systematic measurement pathologies that a forecasting study must
characterise explicitly rather than assume away.

\section{Research Gap and Chapter Summary}

This chapter has covered four bodies of literature: the statistical
characteristics of air quality series that motivate the methodological
choices in Chapter~\ref{chap:method}; classical and machine learning methods
for time series forecasting generally, and why the forecasting-competition
literature predicts a flexible learner need not beat a classical benchmark on
a small sample; deep learning methods for sequences, and the specific
architectural reason a GRU rather than an LSTM suits a dataset this size;
and the two literatures, forecast verification and air quality monitor data
quality, that this project's own findings connect back to directly. Taken
together, this literature places the project's contribution precisely.
Applying an established model suite to Delhi's air quality problem is not
new, and neither is the finding that classical methods hold their ground
against machine learning on a modest sample. What the Delhi-specific studies
above do not do is evaluate that comparison as a warning system with an
explicit, varying alarm budget, using verification methodology from a
literature that reaches air quality forecasting only indirectly.
Chapter~\ref{chap:results} shows why that omission matters: the ranking of
models looks different once accuracy is separated from operational
usefulness, a finding neither literature taken alone would have anticipated.

\chapter{Methodology}
\label{chap:method}

\section{Research Design}

This chapter proceeds from data to model to evaluation. Section~\ref{sec:data}
describes the data source and the station-selection process.
Section~\ref{sec:preprocess} describes two defects found in the raw series,
the seasonality analysis that overturned an assumption in the approved
proposal, and the feature table built from the cleaned series.
Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods} and Section~\ref{sec:dl-methods} give the full
mathematical specification of the two families of model this project
compares, machine learning and deep learning, each covering the method's
general form before the specific configuration used here.
Section~\ref{sec:rolling} specifies the rolling-origin evaluation every model
is scored under, and Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures} specifies the accuracy
and warning-system measures reported in Chapter~\ref{chap:results}.

\section{Data Collection and Station Selection}
\label{sec:data}

Daily mean PM$_{2.5}$ concentrations were obtained from OpenAQ. Five candidate
monitoring stations within 25\,km of central Delhi were compared on data
coverage rather than on nominal length of record.

The comparison produced an unexpected constraint. Every station operated by the
Central Pollution Control Board returns measurements only from 19 February 2025,
approximately eighteen months, although the OpenAQ location metadata advertises a
first observation in February 2016. Four independent stations sharing an
identical cutoff indicates a systematic limit on what the measurements endpoint
serves rather than a coincidence. Only location 8118 returns the full record and
it was therefore selected.

This carries a limitation that must be stated plainly. Location 8118 is supplied
through AirNow and is a United States diplomatic post monitor rather than part of
the Indian official network. The project therefore forecasts at a single
well-characterised reference site in Delhi, which is common in this literature,
and the results should not be read as representative of the city as a whole.

\section{Data Preprocessing}
\label{sec:preprocess}

\subsection{Data Cleaning: Two Defects in the Source Data}
\label{sec:defects}

Two problems were identified before any modelling, one of which was silently
corrupting the series.

\paragraph{Physically impossible values.} The raw series contained five negative
concentrations and a maximum of 1990\,\textmu g\,m$^{-3}$. The value 1990.0
appeared three times identically on unrelated dates, which is the signature of a
clipped instrument ceiling rather than a measurement. One occurrence fell on 2
September, during the monsoon, between neighbouring days of 42 and 178.

\paragraph{An incorrect coverage denominator.} OpenAQ reports the completeness of
each daily aggregate as the observation count divided by an expected count of 24,
assuming hourly reporting. The sensor at location 8118 reported half-hourly from
2016 to 2024 and hourly from 2025 onward. The visible symptom is a reported
completeness exceeding 100 per cent, which is impossible. The damaging symptom is
invisible: a day holding 24 of a genuine 48 readings is scored as fully complete,
so a mean computed from half a day of a polluted afternoon enters the series as
though it were a daily mean. Days at 50 to 75 per cent true coverage produced
implausible values approximately seven times as often as days above 90 per cent,
which identifies incomplete days as the mechanism rather than a coincidence.

The correction takes the reporting cadence from the data, using the ninetieth
percentile of observation counts within each year, which follows the 2025 change
in reporting interval automatically. Recomputed on that basis, 1{,}085 of the
3{,}467 raw calendar-linked days fall below 75 per cent true coverage, far more
than the 268 days that have no recorded value at all and would be the only ones
flagged by a check for whether a value exists rather than how reliably it was
measured.

\centering
\caption{Cleaning rules applied, and the basis for each.}
\label{tab:cleaning}
\input{tables/cleaning}
\end{table}

The coverage threshold is set at 50 per cent rather than a stricter value because
the longest gap is the binding constraint: at 60 per cent the worst gap rises to
69 days and at 90 per cent to 185 days, either of which would distort estimation
of the annual cycle. At 50 per cent the worst gap is 34 days. The exceedance rate
moves only from 30.0 to 27.0 per cent across every candidate threshold, which
confirms that the filter is not selectively removing the events of interest.

solid line and the fixed denominator of 24 as the dashed line. Panel (b) shows

\subsection{Seasonality Analysis}
\label{sec:weekly}

The approved proposal states that daily pollution series carry a weekly cycle
driven by traffic and industrial activity, and treats the coexistence of a weekly
and an annual period as the central modelling difficulty, since a seasonal ARIMA
accommodates only one seasonal period.

Tested on the cleaned series, the weekly cycle is not present at this station.
Three independent tests agree. The periodogram gives dominant periods of 357.9,
178.9, 188.4, 397.7, 325.4 and 60.7 days, which is the annual cycle and its
harmonics, with nothing near seven. On the deseasonalised logarithm of
concentration the autocorrelation at lag 7 is 0.173, while lag 6 is 0.179 and lag
8 is 0.153, so lag 7 lies on the decay curve rather than above it; the same holds
at lags 14 and 21. The day of week effect on the same residuals spans 6.5 per
cent between the highest and lowest day, with an analysis of variance giving
$F = 1.13$, $p = 0.34$ and a Kruskal-Wallis test giving $p = 0.77$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig3_weekly}
\caption{No weekly cycle. Lags 7, 14 and 21 are circled and lie on the decay
curve rather than above it. Every day of week interval contains zero.}
\label{fig:weekly}
\end{figure}

There is a physical reading rather than a null result. A weekly rhythm in urban
particulate concentration is a traffic signature, and location 8118 sits in the
diplomatic enclave rather than at a roadside site such as ITO or Anand Vihar. Its
absence at a site that is not traffic dominated is what one would expect.

The consequence for the specification is direct: the classical benchmark is ARIMA
with annual Fourier terms as exogenous regressors and no weekly seasonal order.
The specification is simpler, better identified, and empirically justified rather
than assumed.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.66\textwidth]{figures/fig4_annual}
\caption{The annual cycle, by contrast, is unmistakable: monthly median with the
interquartile range shaded. Its strength is what makes the absence in
Figure~\ref{fig:weekly} credible rather than an artefact of a weak test.}
\label{fig:annual}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Feature Construction}
\label{sec:features}

A supervised table was built with one row per forecast origin. A row indexed by
date $t$ carries only functions of observations up to and including day $t$, and
its targets are the concentrations on days $t+1$, $t+2$ and $t+3$. Features
comprise lags at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 7 days; first differences; rolling mean, standard
deviation and maximum over 3, 7, 14 and 30 days; an anomaly and standardised
anomaly against the 30 day norm; exceedance frequency over the last 7 and 30
days; days since the last exceedance; calendar terms; four pairs of annual
Fourier terms; and three missingness indicators.

Missing values are never imputed. Gradient boosting accepts them natively and the
state space models skip the measurement update at a gap, so the absence is
carried as information rather than replaced by a fabricated value. The single
exception is the recurrent network, discussed in Section~\ref{sec:gru}.

\section{Machine Learning Methods}
\label{sec:ml-methods}

Six of the ten specifications fitted in this project belong to the machine
learning family in the broad sense used in Section~\ref{sec:lit-ml}: the
classical ARIMA benchmark, which is included here for comparison even though
it predates the term, and the three explicitly machine learning regressors,
each fitted to both the level of concentration and its change from the
forecast origin. Every model in this section is fitted to the logarithm of
concentration rather than the raw scale. Annual Fourier terms explain 69 per
cent of the variance of the logarithm against considerably less on the raw
scale, and fitting in logs prevents a model predicting a negative
concentration, which has no physical meaning.

\subsection{Classical Benchmark: ARIMA with Fourier Terms}
\label{sec:arima}

Let $y_t = \log(\text{PM2.5}_t)$ and let $B$ denote the backshift operator,
$B y_t = y_{t-1}$. An autoregressive integrated moving average model of order
$(p,d,q)$ with exogenous regressors $x_t$ is
\begin{equation}
\phi(B)\,(1-B)^d y_t \;=\; c \;+\; \theta(B)\,\varepsilon_t \;+\; \beta^\top x_t,
\label{eq:arima}
\end{equation}
where $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \cdots - \phi_p B^p$ is the autoregressive
polynomial, $\theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B + \cdots + \theta_q B^q$ is the moving
average polynomial, and $\varepsilon_t$ is white noise. The order selected
from an explicit grid by the Akaike information criterion on the training
block is $(p,d,q) = (1,1,1)$, so Equation~\ref{eq:arima} specialises to
\begin{equation}
(1 - \phi_1 B)(1-B)\,y_t \;=\; c \;+\; (1+\theta_1 B)\,\varepsilon_t \;+\;
\sum_{k=1}^{4}\Big[\alpha_k \sin\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi k t}{365.25}\Big) +
\beta_k \cos\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi k t}{365.25}\Big)\Big],
\label{eq:arima-fourier}
\end{equation}
with four pairs of annual Fourier terms ($K=4$) as the exogenous regressors
$x_t$, carrying the annual cycle established in Section~\ref{sec:weekly} and
deliberately carrying no weekly seasonal order.

Back-transformation from the log scale is not innocent. If $\log y$ has
forecast mean $m$ and forecast variance $s^2$, then under the model's
Gaussian error assumption $y$ is lognormally distributed, and
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{median}(y) = \exp(m), \qquad \mathrm{mean}(y) = \exp\!\big(m + \tfrac{1}{2}s^2\big).
\label{eq:lognormal}
\end{equation}
Both quantities were produced as separately named models, since a report
that back-transforms without stating which one it reports has silently
changed what is being forecast.

\subsection{Penalised Linear Regression}

Given the feature matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ built in
Section~\ref{sec:features} and the target vector $y$, ordinary least squares
is unstable when predictors are highly correlated, as lagged and
rolling-window features of the same series necessarily are. Ridge regression
\citep{hoerl1970ridge} controls this by penalising the size of the
coefficient vector:
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta} \; \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 \;+\; \lambda \|\beta\|_2^2,
\label{eq:ridge}
\end{equation}
with closed-form solution $\hat\beta = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y$.
The penalty $\lambda > 0$ shrinks the coefficients toward zero, trading a
small increase in bias for a reduction in variance; $\lambda$ is selected by
cross-validation on the training block at every refit.

\subsection{Random Forest}

A random forest \citep{breiman2001random} fits $B$ regression trees to
independent bootstrap resamples of the training data, each tree considering
only a random subset of features at every split, and averages their
predictions:
\begin{equation}
\hat f(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x).
\label{eq:rf}
\end{equation}
Each tree $T_b$ is grown by recursively partitioning the feature space: at a
node with data $\{(x_i,y_i)\}$, the split $(j,s)$ on feature $j$ at threshold
$s$ is chosen to minimise the total within-region sum of squared error,
\begin{equation}
\min_{j,s} \; \left[ \sum_{i\,:\,x_{ij} \le s} (y_i - \bar y_{R_1})^2 \;+\;
\sum_{i\,:\,x_{ij} > s} (y_i - \bar y_{R_2})^2 \right],
\label{eq:rf-split}
\end{equation}
where $R_1$ and $R_2$ are the two resulting regions and $\bar y_{R_1}$,
$\bar y_{R_2}$ their mean targets. Averaging over many such trees, each
trained on a different resample and a different random subset of features at
each split, reduces the variance of a single tree's prediction without
imposing a linear functional form.

\subsection{Histogram Gradient Boosting}

Gradient boosting \citep{friedman2001gradient} fits an ensemble additively
rather than by averaging independent trees. The ensemble is initialised as a
constant, $F_0(x) = \arg\min_{\gamma} \sum_i L(y_i,\gamma)$, and for
$m = 1,\dots,M$ a regression tree $h_m$ is fitted to the negative gradient of
the loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions,
\begin{equation}
r_{im} \;=\; -\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i,F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F=F_{m-1}},
\label{eq:grad-residual}
\end{equation}
which for squared-error loss reduces to the ordinary residual
$r_{im} = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$, and the ensemble is updated by
\begin{equation}
F_m(x) \;=\; F_{m-1}(x) \;+\; \nu\, h_m(x),
\label{eq:boost-update}
\end{equation}
where $0 < \nu \le 1$ is a shrinkage (learning rate) parameter that controls
how much each new tree is allowed to correct the ensemble. The
histogram-based implementation used here bins continuous features before
searching for splits, which accepts missing values natively, consistent with
the decision in Section~\ref{sec:features} never to impute. Both the number
of boosting iterations $M$ and the per-tree leaf count were chosen at every
refit from a small explicit grid, since an uncontrolled $M$ overfits badly on
a series of this length, a failure mode encountered and corrected during
development and reported in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.

Both the random forest and the gradient boosting models were fitted twice,
once to the level of log concentration and once to its change from the
forecast origin, since a tree cannot extrapolate beyond the range of targets
it was trained on and this series drifts across the decade of record;
modelling the change removes that handicap by asking the tree to represent a
roughly stationary residual rather than a trending level.

\section{Deep Learning Methods}
\label{sec:dl-methods}

\subsection{The Gated Recurrent Unit: Architecture and Training}
\label{sec:gru}

The gated recurrent unit \citep{cho2014gru} maintains a hidden state
$h_t \in \mathbb{R}^H$ updated at each timestep $t$ by two gates. The update
gate $z_t$ controls how much of the previous state is retained against how
much is replaced by a new candidate state; the reset gate $r_t$ controls how
much of the previous state is used in forming that candidate:
\begin{align}
z_t &= \sigma\big(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z\big), \label{eq:gru-z}\\
r_t &= \sigma\big(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r\big), \label{eq:gru-r}\\
\tilde h_t &= \tanh\big(W_h x_t + U_h (r_t \odot h_{t-1}) + b_h\big), \label{eq:gru-htilde}\\
h_t &= (1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1} \;+\; z_t \odot \tilde h_t, \label{eq:gru-h}
\end{align}
where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid, $\odot$ is elementwise
multiplication, and $W_z,W_r,W_h,U_z,U_r,U_h,b_z,b_r,b_h$ are the parameters
learned by training. Because the final state $h_t$ in Equation~\ref{eq:gru-h}
is a convex combination of the previous state and the new candidate rather
than a product of many successive nonlinear transformations, gradients can
flow backward through many timesteps without vanishing, which is the
property that motivated gated architectures in Section~\ref{sec:lit-dl}.

The specific network fitted in this project is a single GRU layer with
$H=24$ hidden units, reading a sequence of the last 30 days
($t-29,\dots,t$), each day carrying three channels: the logarithm of
concentration, a missingness flag, and the annual Fourier terms from
Section~\ref{sec:features}. A linear output layer maps the final hidden state
$h_t$ to a single predicted value, the change in log concentration from the
forecast origin, with the origin value added back afterwards; modelling the
change rather than the level is the same device used for the tree models in
Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods}, for the same reason. The network is trained by
minimising mean absolute error with the Adam optimiser, with early stopping
on a chronological holdout, the most recent 15 per cent of each training
window, so that training stops once validation error no longer improves
rather than at a fixed epoch count.

A recurrent network forces a compromise that no other model in this project
requires. It must be handed a value at every timestep: it cannot skip one the
way the state space model in Section~\ref{sec:arima} skips a measurement
update, and it cannot accept a missing value the way the histogram gradient
boosting model in Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods} can. Gaps are therefore carried
forward in the log-concentration channel, with the separate missingness flag
marking which days were filled rather than observed. The one architecture
Dr Tian specifically asked to be included is the one architecture in the
suite that cannot represent the statement that a value is unknown.

Because the network's weights are initialised randomly, its forecast depends
on that initialisation, unlike every other model in this project. It is
therefore fitted independently across five random seeds, and its result is
reported throughout Chapter~\ref{chap:results} as the range across those
five runs, never as a single seed's point estimate; the justification for
treating this as a reporting requirement rather than a presentational choice
is given in Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}.

\section{Rolling-Origin Evaluation}
\label{sec:rolling}

Every model was evaluated over 2{,}303 origins from 9 November 2019 to 24 August
2026, spanning 6.8 years, with a three year burn-in, parameters re-estimated
every 90 days and model state advanced daily in between.

This is not a refinement of a single train-test split; it replaces one, for the
reason standard cross-validation is inappropriate for dependent data in the
first place: shuffling origins lets a model trained on the future score itself
against the past \citep{bergmeir2012crossvalidation}. On a single test block the
ARIMA scored 0.940 in relative terms at one day ahead against 0.903 on the
single block, because that block happened to be calmer than the training
period and was flattering every model. A single split is one draw from a
process, and a conclusion drawn from it is a conclusion about that period.

The governing invariant is that at origin $t$ a model may use observations up to
and including day $t$ and nothing else: not the value at $t+1$, not a parameter
estimated using data after $t$, and not a scaling constant or imputed value
computed from the full series. Since nothing fails visibly when that is broken,
and the numbers merely improve, the invariant is enforced by construction and
tested directly. Every model runs through one shared loop, and that loop is
verified by corrupting the series from a chosen date, rerunning, and requiring
that no forecast issued before that date changes.

One trap is specific to supervised learning under a rolling origin. At origin $t$
the label attached to feature row $t'$ is the concentration at $t' + h$, so the
training set ends at $t - h$ rather than at $t$. A separate model is fitted per
horizon because that arithmetic requires it. The error would have amounted to
three rows per refit and would have been entirely invisible in the output.

\section{Evaluation Measures}
\label{sec:evalmeasures}

Accuracy is reported separately at each horizon and never averaged, since skill
decays with horizon and concealing that would defeat the purpose. The headline
measure is relative mean absolute error against the persistence forecast computed
on identical rows, so that 1.000 is persistence and values below one beat it.
Mean absolute scaled error is reported alongside, but it divides by the training
period volatility and therefore also reflects any difference in volatility
between periods, which is material here.

As a warning system, a day is an event if the observed concentration exceeds the
health threshold, and an alarm is raised when the forecast exceeds a decision
threshold. These are separate quantities and are kept separate throughout.
Reported are the hit rate, the false alarm rate defined as false alarms divided
by quiet days, precision, the critical success index, and alarms raised per year.
The last is included because a false alarm rate of 0.10 sounds negligible and
means roughly one wasted alarm every ten quiet days, which is what an operator
actually experiences.

\section{Reproducibility}

The analysis runs end to end from an empty directory in thirteen command line
scripts, each carrying an automated correctness test that runs before it
produces any output. The rolling origin harness verifies its own leakage
invariant before every run. Every table in this report is generated directly
from the result files by \texttt{make\_tables.py}; no number has been
transcribed by hand. Raw and cleaned data are held under version control so
that the analysis does not depend on the data provider serving identical
values at a later date, which the finding in Section~\ref{sec:data} suggests
is not a safe assumption. The complete repository, including every commit
from initial data acquisition to this report, is public and runnable at
\texttt{github.com/JC16092/mth5000-aqi-forecast}.

\section{Chapter Summary}

This chapter described the data, two defects found in it, and the feature
table built from it, and then gave the full mathematical specification of
the two method families compared in this project. Machine learning, in
Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods}, comprises a classical ARIMA benchmark and three
regressors, ridge, random forest, and gradient boosting, each controlling
the bias-variance trade-off by a different mechanism: shrinkage, bagging, or
additive stagewise correction. Deep learning, in Section~\ref{sec:dl-methods},
comprises a single gated recurrent network, whose gating mechanism is
specifically what lets it avoid the vanishing-gradient failure of a plain
recurrent network. Every model is evaluated under the same rolling-origin
protocol, specified in Section~\ref{sec:rolling}, and scored by the same
measures, specified in Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures}, so that the comparison
in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} is a fair one.

\chapter{Results and Analysis}
\label{chap:results}

\section{Forecast Accuracy}
\label{sec:results-rq1}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Relative mean absolute error against persistence, under rolling origin
evaluation over 2{,}303 origins. Lower is better and 1.000 is persistence. The
recurrent network is given as the range over five initialisation seeds; it is the
only model whose result depends on one.}
\label{tab:accuracy}
\footnotesize
\input{tables/accuracy}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} answers the first research question, and the answer is
not uniform across horizons.

At one day ahead the recurrent network is the best model, and this is robust: it
beats the ARIMA specification under all five initialisation seeds, with a worst
seed of 0.935 against 0.940. At two days the ARIMA is better under all five
seeds, though by 0.003 against the best of them. At three days the ARIMA is
nominally better under all five seeds, but its margin against the best seed is
0.0003, which is a tie in any language that would survive examination.

The mechanism is coherent. At one day ahead the forecast is dominated by
short-range structure, where a nonlinear model has something to exploit. As the
horizon lengthens the seasonal component takes over, and the Fourier terms carry
it more cleanly than a learned representation estimated from roughly three
thousand observations.

The network is reported as a range rather than a point because it is the only
model whose result depends on a random initialisation, and the dependence is not
small. Across seeds the spread is 0.019 at one day, 0.013 at two and 0.047 at
three. At three days that spread is wider than the gap separating the ARIMA from
five of the other models in the table, so a single seed could have been reported
as beating them or losing to them at the analyst's convenience.

Two subsidiary results support the specification choices. Removing the Fourier
terms from the ARIMA degrades it by 3.3 points of relative error at one day and
by 5.8 points at three, under the same rolling-origin harness, so the seasonal
terms earn their place and increasingly so with horizon. Modelling the change
from the origin rather than the level improves
both tree models, because a tree cannot extrapolate beyond the targets it was
trained on and this series drifts downward across the decade.

\section{Two Arms of the Same Question}

Neither arm dominates. Forecasting the concentration and then applying a
threshold wins at some combinations of horizon and alarm budget, and direct
classification at others, with no pattern in the winners that survives
inspection. Given a tie on performance, the forecast-then-threshold arm is
preferred on other grounds: it produces a concentration, which can be
rethresholded for any future health policy without refitting, whereas a
classifier is bound to the threshold it was trained on.

\section{The Decision Threshold}
\label{sec:threshold}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Best hit rate available within a budget of alarms per year, with the
event fixed at the health threshold and only the decision threshold varying.}
\label{tab:budget}
\footnotesize
\input{tables/budget}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:budget} contains the principal result of this project. Moving the
alarm budget from 40 to 100 per year changes the achievable hit rate at one day
ahead from 0.377 to 0.873. Holding the budget fixed and changing the model
instead moves it by around five points.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig5_warning}
\caption{The trade-off, by horizon. The top row shows hit rate against false
alarm rate; the bottom row replaces the false alarm rate with alarms raised per
year, the unit in which an operator budgets. The curves very nearly coincide,
which is the finding. They have deliberately not been separated for legibility.}
\label{fig:warning}
\end{figure}

Two individual comparisons make the point sharper than the aggregate does. At a
budget of 100 alarms per year and one day ahead, persistence achieves a hit rate
of 0.873, which is the best figure any model in the study achieves at that budget.
At three days ahead and a budget of 60, a climatological forecast, which uses no
recent information whatever, matches the best model to within four thousandths.
Figure~\ref{fig:warning} shows the same result as curves; they very nearly
coincide, and they have deliberately not been separated for legibility.

The reading is not that modelling is pointless. It is that the quantity a
decision maker controls, namely how many alarms per year can be justified,
dominates the quantity a modeller controls. A report that presents a model
comparison without stating the operating point it was evaluated at has answered a
question nobody asked.

\section{Chapter Summary}

Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} answers the first research question with a
horizon-dependent result: the deep learning model wins at one day ahead, the
classical model wins or ties beyond it. Section~\ref{sec:threshold} answers
the third, and it is the result the rest of this report is organised around:
the alarm budget, not the model, is what principally determines warning
performance. Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion} takes up what that means in
practice.

% ============================================================================
\chapter{Discussion}
\label{chap:discussion}

\section{The Operational Question Dominates the Modelling Question}

Table~\ref{tab:budget} and Figure~\ref{fig:warning} together make a single
point, and this section states what follows from it rather than repeating the
numbers. A decision maker who fixes how many alarms per year an operator or
the public will tolerate has more influence over how many hazardous days are
caught than a modeller choosing among the ten specifications fitted in this
project. Moving the budget from 40 to 100 alarms a year moves the achievable
hit rate at one day ahead from 0.377 to 0.873, a range of fifty points.
Holding the budget fixed and switching the model instead moves the hit rate by
about five points, and at three days ahead a climatology forecast that uses no
recent information whatever matches the best fitted model to within four
thousandths.

This is not an argument against modelling. ARIMA and the recurrent network
both earn real, if modest, gains over persistence in Table~\ref{tab:accuracy},
and a better point forecast still narrows the range of thresholds worth
considering. It is an argument about where the leverage in this problem
actually sits. A hazardous air quality warning system is not a machine
learning benchmark with a threshold attached to it afterwards; the threshold
is the policy instrument, and the forecasting model only supplies its input.
A comparison of models that does not first fix the alarm budget it was
evaluated at has answered a question nobody who has to operate the system
actually asked. The practical recommendation that follows is to treat the
alarm budget as the primary subject of discussion with the health authority
commissioning such a system, and the choice of forecasting model as a
secondary refinement of a curve whose shape is already mostly fixed by what
every model in this study shares: the persistence of concentration from one
day to the next, and the annual cycle.

\section{How Large Is a Difference Between Models?}

Two results in this project bound that question from below. Running the identical
pipeline on two different machines moved the tree models by up to 0.004 in
relative error, because histogram gradient boosting parallelises with OpenMP and
floating point summation order depends on the thread count. Changing only the
random initialisation of the recurrent network moved it by 0.013 to 0.047.

Several of the gaps between adjacent models in Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} are of
that order. Any claim that one of those models is better than another, made
without stating the run to run variation, is not supported by the evidence.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The analysis rests on a single monitor, OpenAQ location 8118, which
Section~\ref{sec:data} shows is supplied through AirNow and is almost
certainly a United States diplomatic post instrument rather than a station in
the Central Pollution Control Board network. It was chosen because it is the
only nearby monitor with a complete decade of record, against the eighteen
months every CPCB station returns; the choice buys history at the cost of
representativeness. The absence of a weekly cycle documented in
Section~\ref{sec:weekly} is consistent with a diplomatic enclave rather than a
roadside site, which supports this reading of the limitation rather than
leaving it an unrelated coincidence, but it does not change the fact that
every number in this report describes one point in the city rather than Delhi
as a whole.

The project forecasts one city. Delhi was chosen because its air quality
problem is severe and well documented, not because it is representative of
Indian cities generally. Pollution sources, meteorology, and the strength of
the seasonal cycle that drives the Fourier terms in Section~\ref{sec:weekly}
all vary by region, and a coastal city or one without a dominant biomass
burning season could show a different balance between the classical and
machine learning models, or a genuine weekly cycle where this station shows
none. Nothing in this report should be read as a claim about any station or
city other than the one it was fitted to.

The upper cleaning threshold of 1000\,\textmu g\,m$^{-3}$ is a judgement rather
than a fact, and its effect on the reported conclusions was checked directly
rather than assumed. Restoring the seven days it removes, including the three
identical readings at 1990 diagnosed in Section~\ref{sec:defects} as a clipped
instrument ceiling, gives 3{,}100 usable days and 927 exceedance days rather
than 3{,}093 and 920, a small shift. Refitting the full rolling-origin harness
on this uncapped series leaves the ARIMA specification essentially unchanged,
0.935 against 0.940 at one day ahead and 0.829 against 0.832 at three days,
because working in logarithms and differencing the series absorbs the
contamination. The machine learning models are not so protected. Ridge moves
from a near tie with persistence to a clear loss at one day ahead, 0.997 to
1.118, and gradient boosting on the level target moves from a narrow win over
persistence to a loss at three days, 0.883 to 1.006. The central finding of
Research Question 1, that the classical benchmark beats every machine learning
model at every horizon, therefore does not merely survive removing the
threshold; it strengthens, because the models it beat most narrowly are
precisely the ones most exposed to the uncleaned tail. The threshold matters,
but it matters more to the machine learning suite than to the model this
project ultimately recommends.

Hyperparameters for the tree-based models were chosen at every refit from a
small explicit grid, scored on a held-out slice of the training window taken
in time order, rather than from an exhaustive or Bayesian search. This
followed a real failure during development, in which fixed hyperparameters let
gradient boosting overfit badly enough to score worse than persistence; the
grid search fixed that specific problem, but a small grid can still miss a
configuration that a wider search would find. The machine learning results in
Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} should therefore be read as a lower bound on what
those model classes could achieve with more computation, not as their ceiling.

No meteorological covariate enters any model. Wind speed in particular is a
well established driver of particulate dispersion and is a plausible source
of the short-range structure that lets the recurrent network beat ARIMA at one
day ahead. A version of this project with wind, temperature, and boundary
layer height added to the feature table is the most direct extension; the
\texttt{meteostat} package, which wraps NOAA and GHCN station data, would
supply it without a new data acquisition problem. Its absence here is a scope
decision made to fit the project inside the time available, not a claim that
meteorology is unimportant.

% ============================================================================
\chapter{Conclusion}
\label{chap:conclusion}

\section{Summary of the Study}

This project forecast hazardous PM2.5 days at a single Delhi monitor one to
three days ahead, comparing a classical benchmark against three machine
learning regressors and a deep recurrent network, and evaluating every
specification as a warning system rather than by average error alone. Two
real defects in the source data, a clipped instrument ceiling and a
mischaracterised coverage statistic, were found and corrected before any
model was fitted, and an assumption carried over from the approved proposal,
that the series holds a weekly cycle alongside its annual one, was tested
directly and found false.

\section{Main Conclusions}

Across ten models spanning simple benchmarks, a classical time series model,
four machine learning regressors, and a recurrent network, the spread in
achievable hit rate at a fixed alarm budget is about five percentage points;
the spread across alarm budgets, holding the model fixed, is about fifty. The
choice a decision maker makes about how many alarms per year can be
justified therefore has far more influence on how many hazardous days are
caught than the choice a modeller makes among the specifications fitted
here.

Machine learning earned its place only partially. ARIMA with annual Fourier
terms beats every machine learning regressor at every horizon, a result that
strengthens rather than weakens under the sensitivity analysis in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. The one machine learning method that does win,
the recurrent network, does so only at one day ahead, and only when reported
honestly as a range across five random initialisations rather than as a single
favourable seed. The supervisor's instruction to try several methods rather
than defaulting to ARIMA was the right one: it is what makes the negative
result at two and three days credible, and what surfaces the one day ahead
result that a project restricted to classical methods would never have found.

\section{Future Work}

Two extensions follow directly from the limitations in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. Adding
meteorological covariates, wind speed in particular, is the most direct route
to improving the short horizon forecasts that the recurrent network already
shows have room to improve. Repeating the analysis at a second, independent
station, ideally one inside the Central Pollution Control Board network once
its record lengthens, would test whether the findings here are a property of
Delhi air quality or an artefact of the one diplomatic enclave monitor this
project was restricted to. Until then, the central recommendation stands on
its own: a hazardous air quality warning system should be designed around the
alarm budget its operator can justify, with the forecasting model treated as a
secondary refinement rather than the primary design choice.
